summary: Design/hand-off for Aurora Bridge marketplace listing and on-prem deployment. Discussed packaging approach (Helm + operator), SSO/SAML integration, KMS/KMS compatibility, network connectivity patterns for air-gapped customers, and preliminary performance expectations. Action items include sharing packaging checklist, running a Private runtime benchmark, and scheduling a security deep-dive.
topics: Rollout strategy: canary vs stripe vs immediate
transcript:
[00:00:00] Emma Chen: Okay everyone uh thanks for taking the time. This is Emma from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account, joined by Ravi and Noel from the Eng team. Quick roll call?
[00:00:12] Maya Lopez: Hey this is Maya, CTO at Aurora Bridge here.
[00:00:18] Jonas Berg: Jonas - platform eng.
[00:00:21] Sara Kim: Sara, security.
[00:00:24] Felix Tan: Felix, DevOps.
[00:00:27] Akio Nakamura: Akio, SRE.
[00:00:30] Emma Chen: Great, cool. Goal for today is to walk through the proposed packaging for Redwood listing and also the on-prem deployment patterns for your air-gapped customers, and cover SSO/SAML integration. We'll surface any gaps and agree next steps.
[00:00:45] Maya Lopez: Sounds good.
[00:00:47] Ravi Patel: Quick note: I'll go over the runtime expectations and a simple benchmark plan so you can see latency/cost tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
[00:00:58] Jonas Berg: One thing up front — our enterprise customers have strict KMS requirements and often want HSM-backed keys, plus some require per-tenant key rotation. Is that supported with your private offering?
[00:01:12] Noel Martinez: Short answer yes, we integrate with customer KMS and HSM via standard interfaces; for the Private package we provide hooks for Cloud KMS or on-prem HSM. The integration path can be either direct KMS calls from the Redwood control plane (if allowed) or we ship an agent that handles key ops inside customer network. There was a small note about firewall rules.
[00:01:29] Sara Kim: When you say agent — is it pulling keys out across the internet or does it stay completely internal? That's a hard req for some customers.
[00:01:36] Ravi Patel: Good question. For air-gapped or restricted environments we recommend the agent-only flow: the agent handles encryption and decryption and never exfiltrates plaintext keys. We can provide an HSM connector that runs in the customer's VPC or on-prem HSM network. There is an option to have the control plane do management metadata only.
[00:01:52] Akio Nakamura: Can you describe network connectivity patterns? We have customers that only allow outbound to a very small set of IPs or require proxy.
[00:01:59] Noel Martinez: Yeah we mapped three patterns: 1) Fully hosted — standard egress to Redwood endpoints, 2) VPC peering or private link — we support private networking to minimize public egress, and 3) Air-gapped — we provide an on-prem bundle with an operator/helm chart that runs locally and syncs artifacts via a signed bundle you pull in. The signed bundle avoids outbound streaming during inference.
[00:02:23] Felix Tan: That bundle — how heavy is it? Will it need GPUs onsite? Most of our customers will want CPU-only reps initially.
[00:02:32] Ravi Patel: The bundle can be configured two ways: a lightweight inference sidecar for small workloads (CPU optimized, quantized models) or a full private runtime that expects GPUs for production-scale. For marketplace listing we recommend shipping both: a 'lite' profile for evaluation and a 'full' profile for production.
[00:02:47] Maya Lopez: About the marketplace packaging — can you run through what you expect in the Helm chart? We have an internal ops template but want to make sure it matches Redwood's listing checks.
[00:02:56] Emma Chen: Absolutely. We'll share a packaging checklist but the highlights — chart values for service type, storage class, model artifact location (s3 or local path for airgapped), secrets schema, KMS connector config, readiness/liveness probes, and a small operator manifest for upgrades. Also a sample values.yaml for 'lite' and 'full' profiles.
[00:03:15] Jonas Berg: Do you require a specific container image topology? We use multi-arch images and we need arm/amd64 support for edge nodes.
[00:03:22] Noel Martinez: We prefer multi-arch but it's not mandatory. For onprem we need at least amd64 for X86 GPU hosts; for edge use cases we do accept arm builds. We'll include a validator script in the listing pipeline that checks image manifests.
[00:03:35] Emma Chen: I'll put the validator sample in the checklist we send.
[00:03:38] Sara Kim: On SSO — our customers use both SAML and OIDC. We also have SCIM for provisioning. How does Redwood handle SSO in marketplace deployments vs Private?
[00:03:48] Ravi Patel: For Hosted it's straightforward — SAML/OIDC integrations through the Redwood Console with SSO configs per account, and SCIM for user provisioning. For Private, if you want the control plane to manage users, we support SAML/OIDC via the customer's IdP through a private control plane endpoint. For fully offline installs we support local auth that syncs via SCIM when connectivity is available, or you can use a pass-through where customer IdP handles the login and the operator maps identities to RBAC.
[00:04:14] Akio Nakamura: Mapping identities — is there a standard for role mapping? We want RBAC to line up with our internal roles.
[00:04:19] Noel Martinez: Yep, we expose role mappings via a CRD or configmap in the operator; for Hosted we have a GUI mapping table.
[00:04:25] Felix Tan: Licensing, billing — if a customer deploys the bundle on-prem and then purchases via marketplace, how does metering work?
[00:04:33] Emma Chen: Two common approaches: licensing token + offline metering where the operator periodically emits usage receipts (signed) that the customer uploads to claim usage, or the customer purchases a subscription in the marketplace and we provide activation keys that unlock features in the operator. For strict compliance, the signed receipts flow is preferred. We'll document both patterns.
[00:04:50] Maya Lopez: Let's talk about performance expectations. Our customers ask about cold-starts and token-level latency. Do you have numbers for the Private runtime?
[00:04:58] Ravi Patel: Preliminary numbers depend on model size and quantization. For a 7B model quantized we typically see tail latencies in the 200-350ms per token range on a T4-equivalent GPU with batching tuned. Cold-start token latency (first response) can be higher because KV cache init — think 800ms to 1.2s if the model wasn't warm. We'll run a focused test with your sample model to give concrete numbers.
[00:05:22] Jonas Berg: Can you include memory and disk requirements in the test output? We need to plan node sizing.
[00:05:27] Ravi Patel: Absolutely. I'll include peak GPU memory, average CPU, and local disk footprint. Also a quick note: enabling prefix/KV caching will reduce per-token latency for repeated contexts, but it increases memory usage per instance.
[00:05:40] Sara Kim: Any exportable audit logs for compliance? We need immutable logs for model inputs/outputs transformed or redacted.
[00:05:47] Noel Martinez: We capture audit trails with optional PII scrubbing. For Private we can ship logs to your SIEM or write them locally with signed checksums. The control plane can also store immutable event logs if the customer allows it.
[00:06:00] Maya Lopez: A specific ask from our compliance team: can you support customer-managed key rotation on a schedule without downtime?
[00:06:08] Ravi Patel: Yes, we support rolling key rotation with zero downtime when configured with the HSM connector; the operator coordinates staged key rollout so active inference sessions keep using the previous key until new sessions pick up rotated key. We'll detail the sequence in a KB.
[00:06:24] Felix Tan: About upgrades — if we push a new model or runtime, what's the recommended rollout? Canary? Blue/green?
[00:06:31] Emma Chen: Redwood recommends canary for model changes and blue/green for runtime major upgrades. For marketplace listings we include a canary manifest sample that uses percentage traffic routing and automatic rollback based on error budget traces.
[00:06:44] Jonas Berg: One of the enterprise buyers asked about fallbacks — if a GPU node fails, can traffic route automatically to a hosted fallback?
[00:06:52] Noel Martinez: Yes that's part of graceful degradation. The smart routing policy can failover to a hosted or dedicated pool based on policy (latency and data residency allowances). We'll show policy examples in the docs.
[00:07:04] Akio Nakamura: Okay good.
[00:07:07] Emma Chen: We'll share a short bundle: packaging checklist, sample helm charts for lite/full, validator script, and a stubbed RBAC mapping CRD. Also Ravi will run the perf test. Noel will schedule security deep-dive.
[00:07:20] Maya Lopez: I just want to flag that for some customers data residency is required — EU only. Can the marketplace listing indicate region-limited deployments and provide a region filter?
[00:07:30] Emma Chen: Yes, listings can include metadata tags for region constraints; on the Private side we support region-aware image registries and region locking in the operator.
[00:07:37] Sara Kim: One small nit — the docs should include firewall port lists and example iptables rules for air-gapped prep.
[00:07:43] Noel Martinez: Noted, we'll add a 'network prep' section with iptables examples and proxy env var templates.
[00:07:50] Felix Tan: Any gotchas we should know when converting our internal manifests to your validator? We use kustomize overlays heavily.
[00:07:58] Ravi Patel: The validator supports both Helm and Kustomize. For overlays we'll include an example on how to render and feed the manifest into the validator which checks for required annotations and secrets schema.
[00:08:09] Maya Lopez: Alright, sounds good. Final ask: share the checklist and let's get a follow-up for perf and security.
[00:08:16] Emma Chen: Yep — next steps as discussed. Thanks everyone.
[00:08:20] Jonas Berg: Thanks.
[00:08:22] Sara Kim: Thanks all.
[00:08:24] [meeting end]

Notes: transcript contains some ASR noise; product names occasionally mis-transcribed (e.g., 'K-V cash' instead of "KV cache").
